local_facts.claim: Colorado law makes irretrievable breakdown of the marriage relationship the sole basis for dissolution. A petition for dissolution must allege that the marriage is irretrievably broken.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The statutory basis for a Colorado divorce is different from proving marital misconduct. That rule does not resolve the separate questions about property, debt, parenting, support, disclosures, or an agreement in a particular case.
local_facts.title: Colorado’s divorce standard is irretrievable breakdown

local_facts.claim: Colorado Judicial Branch instructions say a divorce has a 91-day waiting period even if spouses agree on all issues. The period begins when a joint petition is filed, or when the other spouse is served or signs a waiver in a separately filed matter.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Ninety-one days is a minimum court period, not a promise that a case will be finished on that date. Filing, service, financial documents, court directions, agreements, disagreements, and scheduling can affect the path after a case begins.
local_facts.title: The 91-day period is a minimum, not a completion date

local_facts.claim: Denver District Court handles domestic-relations cases, including dissolution of marriage. Colorado’s filing instructions say each spouse must file a Sworn Financial Statement and Certificate of Compliance within 42 days after filing or receiving the petition; Denver also publishes local family-law forms for use in Denver District Court only.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A Denver matter can involve both statewide Colorado requirements and Denver-only court materials. Organizing financial records and checking the correct court’s instructions helps prevent a form or timing detail from being overlooked.
local_facts.title: Denver cases use statewide rules and Denver court materials

anchors.label: Fee contingent on securing the divorce
anchors.detail: No contingent fee agreement may be made in a domestic relations matter where payment turns on securing a divorce or on the amount of maintenance, child support, or property settlement in lieu of those amounts.

anchors.label: Petition for divorce, legal separation or annulment
anchors.detail: Statutory filing fee published by the Colorado Judicial Branch under C.R.S. 13-32-101. A response is $146 and a petition for allocation of parental responsibilities is $252.
anchors.source_name: Colorado Judicial Branch list of fees

anchors.label: Court-connected mediation, each party
anchors.detail: The Office of Dispute Resolution charges each party that rate for mediation, case preparation and preparing the memorandum of understanding, and a neutral may collect a two-hour advance deposit.
anchors.source_name: Colorado Judicial Branch ODR policies and procedures

anchors.label: Order making one spouse pay the other's fees
anchors.detail: After considering the financial resources of both parties, the court may order a party to pay a reasonable amount of the other party's fees and costs, including work done before filing or after judgment.

fee_rows.stage: A fee tied to the outcome
fee_rows.note: The bar reaches payment contingent on securing the divorce and payment sized by the maintenance, support or property figure. It is not a bar on every arrangement in a family case.
The comment to the rule states the prohibition does not preclude a contingent fee for recovering post-judgment balances due under support, maintenance or other financial orders.

Paragraph (b) requires the basis or rate of the fee, the expenses the client owes, and the scope of the representation communicated in writing before or within a reasonable time after starting, and changes in writing too.
Advances of unearned fees belong to the client and stay in trust until a benefit is conferred, and paragraph (g) prohibits nonrefundable fees and nonrefundable retainers.
Petition, response, and a motion to modify a decree or final order filed more than sixty days after it entered. Registering a foreign decree is $201.
fee_rows.source_name: Colorado Judicial Branch list of fees

fee_rows.note: Billed by the Office of Dispute Resolution with a possible two-hour deposit, and up to two hours chargeable for a late cancellation or a no-show. Private mediators set their own rates.
